articles.title: Debate Settled! Is It Safe to Eat an Egg If It Cracked in the Carton?
articles.content:
As a mom, I rarely have the luxury of grocery shopping by myself. Instead, I almost always have one or two kids doing laps around the shopping cart and asking me to open snacks I have yet to pay for—all while I’m feeling avocados to try to find some that are ripe enough to eat that night. So naturally, I sometimes forget to open the egg carton to check for cracked shells as I’m cruising down the dairy aisle.
Which has led me to wonder: Do I really need to throw away eggs that are already cracked before I bring them home? And how about eggs that accidentally break on the way home? I mean, it’s not like I’m going to eat them raw—they’re going to get cooked. I would hate to throw them out if I didn’t have to, both because eggs are so darn expensive these days and because chucking a few would require me to head back to the grocery store sooner than I want to. That said, I also don’t want to accidentally poison my entire family.
So what’s safe, and what’s not? To get the answer, I spoke with Martin Bucknavage, a retired food-safety specialist. Read on to find out if it’s safe to eat an egg that has cracked in the carton—or if you really need to toss it.

Pretty clean! And that’s because eggs are cleaned before they’re put in the carton. “There is a common practice that involves a wash with an alkaline solution, a light scrub, a sanitizing rinse and then drying them with forced air,” Bucknavage explains.
According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), this washing procedure is required before the USDA can give the eggs a grade, which is that “USDA Grade A” or “Grade AA” you’ll see on most egg cartons in grocery stores. It’s also the reason why you don’t need to (and really shouldn’t) wash eggs at home before you use them, as repeatedly wetting the shells can make them porous enough for bacteria to sneak through.
Still, the cleanliness of the shell is not necessarily the concern when it comes to cracks.
No, it’s not. “The shell is the protective package, so any crack that has occurred opens the opportunity for pathogens or spoilage bacteria to enter,” Bucknavage says. In other words, the shell is keeping the bad guys out. The second it opens, they can start getting in. (More below on that.)
But there must be a little flexibility here, right? Like, a hairline crack you can barely see follows different rules than a full shell cave-in? Nope! Any crack or break, no matter how big or small, creates an opening that bacteria can sneak through, according to Bucknavage.
That said, there is some flexibility when it comes to the timing of the crack. Say you check your carton in the store and your eggs are crack-free, but then the milk falls on top of them in the car and one egg is cracked by the time you get home. “If it cracks on the way home from the store or once at home, it can be used immediately or transferred to a clean container with a seal,” says Bucknavage. The key here is limiting the amount of time the egg spends in the cracked shell. “We do not want to hold that cracked egg as is for any length of time,” Bucknavage explains, “because that crack will allow bacteria to enter and grow.”
According to Bucknavage, if you cook an egg or transfer it to a clean, airtight container within a few hours of the shell cracking, it should be safe to eat or use at a later date. Just keep in mind that you’re on the clock: You can use a cracked egg only for up to two days before it’s no longer advisable.
Again, this is only for shells that you break, not ones you find in the grocery store that way. That’s because there’s no way to tell when they were broken.
An eggshell may have a wide array of bacteria—some totally harmless and some potentially dangerous—colonizing it. There are bacteria living inside the hen, others in the nest or on the farm, others in the packaging and processing portions of the egg’s journey, and still others in the grocery store. In other words, the shell is super important for keeping all this bacteria from getting into the part of the egg that you eat.
The one people tend to worry about the most is salmonella, which research has shown can survive on the surface of an egg for as many as 54 days! If salmonella gets inside the egg and then into your body, it can cause a host of unpleasant digestive symptoms, per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In rare cases, it could lead to extreme illness or even death.
In addition to salmonella, eggshells occasionally play host to other types of bacteria that can make you sick, such as E. coli, staphylococcus, enterococcus, and enterobacteriaceae, according to one study.
It’s a lot to worry about, we know. However, the key to remember in all of these cases is that the biological role of the shell is to protect the egg within from contamination. As long as the shell is intact, it’s going to do this job.
It depends on how you cook it and how much bacteria is present. “In general, you want to cook eggs until the whites and yolks are firm, or cook them in a baked dish to 165 degrees Fahrenheit or higher,” Bucknavage explains. “The problem is that many people like to cook eggs so the yolks are runny. This is fine if no pathogens are present, but cooking like this will not eliminate pathogens, especially if the number of organisms is high.”
So if your egg just cracked and you want to use it, try scrambling it, hard-boiling it or using it in a baking recipe. Save the frying for those that haven’t cracked.
If the egg has been cracked for longer than the few hours mentioned above, you’re better off tossing it. Why? The longer it spends cracked, the more bacteria can enter the egg. And the more bacteria there are present, the harder it is to kill them all off during cooking, even at a high temperature.
Plus, Bucknavage adds, bacteria can enter a cracked egg and spoil it. And while cooking and eating it won’t make you sick, a spoiled egg just isn’t going to taste very good. Case closed!

articles.title: Everyone’s Talking About You Can See Everything—Here’s Why the Twisty Elizabeth Holmes Documentary Is the Movie to Watch This Year
articles.content: If you could turn a camera on yourself in a movie theater, what would you see? If you’re watching the new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything, like I did last week, your face would probably be a mix of shock, bemusement, anger and overall slack-jawed incredulity at how we arrived at this moment in time. Like, what is even happening here? This strange movie about an equally strange character is mesmerizing, just like Holmes’s deep-welled, occasionally blinking blue eyes that have become a fixture over the last decade or so of her rise and fall. It’s a movie you can’t stop starting at, even as you want to avert your gaze, because it raises so many uncomfortable questions about our current moment, what we value and even reality itself. The A24 production, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, opened last weekend with a $15 million box-office haul, the biggest opener for a documentary since Michael Moore’s Fahrenheit 9/11 back in 2004. It did even better in its second weekend, bringing the doc’s two-week total up to $45 million. It’s also generating Oscar buzz and, due to its novel structure and storytelling technique, debate about whether it can even be considered a documentary at all. It’s a film that has everyone talking, and you do not want to miss it. Even though it’s nearly three hours long, I’d see it again right now if I wasn’t working. To get you ready to watch the film or discuss it with your friends, we scoured the web for helpful background info, hot takes and the buzziest debates about You Can See Everything. Read on to learn what all the fuss is about and what it says about our world right now. Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more entertainment, trends, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long. You Can See Everything follows Elizabeth Holmes, the co-founder of Theranos, a company that purported to invent a way to test a single drop of blood for a range of conditions, as she prepares to go to prison for defrauding investors. A darling of the tech industry back in the early 2010s, Holmes was hailed as the youngest female self-made billionaire and became the face of the rapidly emerging confluence of tech and medicine. The title of the documentary comes from a text message Holmes sent to Fielder, who also appears on camera throughout the film. She and her partner, Billy Evans, with whom she shares two young children, invite Fielder into their home in an attempt to rehabilitate her image, giving the filmmaker wide latitude to document their day-to-day lives. “You can totally see everything,” she texts to Fielder. But can we? As the movie unspools, that initial (some might say feigned) openness begins to feel like a pretext—or even duplicitous. If you’re familiar with Nathan Fielder, you might think he’s a curious choice for a celebrity rehab. And you’d be right. He’s best known as the creator and star of Comedy Central’s Nathan for You, a satirical take on those shows where business consultants help struggling companies succeed. His signature deadpan affect is on full display in You Can See Everything, his first full-length documentary, as is his ability to go well beyond the surface to expose something deeper. Still, Holmes’s artifice became confusing during the shoot, even for him. “I remember having this weird experience … where I’m like, she seems so genuine at times,” Fielder told the audience at a New York Film Festival panel discussion. “But then I’m like, no … I know she’s a liar. It was a weird mental thing.” Audiences for You Can See Everything will likely vary widely. It’s for people who remember the Theranos scandal, for those who are more interested in what Fielder is up to here and, of course, for anyone who wants to join in on the biggest conversation of the moment. It’s a quiet film, but there are plenty of times when I legitimately laughed out loud at its audacity. You Can See Everything is hard to describe, but if you like movies that make you think and have a point of view, get yourself to the theater ASAP. Opinions are overwhelmingly positive yet all over the map, with lots of words like bonkers and mind-bending being floated around. It’s everywhere too: Critics can’t get enough, and the internet is going crazy over the film’s inventive and ironic look at tech culture, our always-online viral reality and moviemaking itself. People are gravitating to it because it’s so much more than a documentary about a disgraced tech billionaire. Here are some highlights and links to great discussions about this fascinating movie. Be aware that there are some spoilers here, so jump ahead if needed. Here’s what everyone is saying about You Can See Everything. A24, the production company behind arthouse megahits like Moonlight, Backrooms and Primetime, has another disruptor on its hands here, and it’s perfect for audiences who are looking for something meatier than the latest superhero sequel. One through line running through A24 movies is the tendency to make small, indie films feel relevant to a broad audience, and this one delivers in spades. Variety‘s Owen Gleiberman says You Can See Everything is “everything a great movie should be: an experience unlike one you’ve had before, one that lures and enthralls you, and that leaves you feeling different when it’s over.” He compares the excitement to early rock ‘n’ roll and the 1970s film renaissance, when new and evolving art forms were transcendent. It’s “an ecstatic disruption, an adventure of the spirit, one that wakes you up and startles you, that makes you want to see it again.” Read more on Variety You read that right: You Can See Everything has already shot to the top of multiple Oscar-contender lists, and not in the Best Documentary category (though that’s a possibility too). Could it upend The Odyssey‘s chances? Maybe! A documentary has never even been nominated for Best Picture, which gives you an idea of how transformative this movie is. And it feels particularly relevant in today’s post-truth era, with Holmes insisting she did nothing wrong and Fielder’s astonishment channeling the audience’s disbelief. Of course, Oscar voters are not exactly known for embracing the avant-garde. But like 2020’s Parasite, the first foreign-language film to win Best Picture with its scathing critique of wealth inequality, and last year’s Sinners, a horror flick that nabbed four wins and 16 nominations, You Can See Everything could be another film that drags the Oscars into the modern era. Read more on The Los Angeles Times There is a shocking and rather sad moment in You Can See Everything that gets to the very heart of what Fielder is seeking to answer with this film: Is Holmes lying about her role in the Theranos scandal, or does she really believe that she did nothing wrong? Put another way, are we watching a performance? After pressing Holmes on her insistence that her blood-testing technology works as advertised, which clearly is not true (hence, her pending imprisonment), Fielder shows her Abbott and Costello’s “Who’s on First?” comedy bit, which plays with the idea of communication and misunderstanding. She doesn’t get the nearly century-old joke, just like she doesn’t seem to “get” that her tech really can’t do what she says it can. Or does she? How can two people who are living in the same reality see things so differently? In an era defined by second-guessing what’s real, from social media to politics to technology, “[Fielder’s] film is a self-reflexive study of the inability to act as people expect—of masking and deception,” says Coleman Spilde at Salon. “How much of life is a performance?” Read more on Salon In an era of streaming ubiquity, it’s been hard for studios to capture the attention of audiences who would just as soon stay at home—especially for a three-hour documentary. But in its opening weekend, You Can See Everything sold out more than 2,000 shows and raked in $15 million at just 855 theaters. After expanding to 2,600 theaters in its second weekend, it added another $19.5 million to its tally. Moviegoers are saying it’s one of those shared cultural moments you have to see in a crowd. Just take a quick look at your socials to see videos of packed lobbies and excited viewers who can’t wait to talk about what the heck they just saw. Read more on Mashable and The Guardian If you followed the Theranos scandal in real time, you likely have an unsympathetic opinion of Holmes. But here, both her partner, Evans, and Theranos co-founder Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, who was also convicted of fraud, come off as controlling and dominating. Late in the film, a reveal about Evans’s role in the negotiations, as well as his activities while she’s in prison, raise questions about who is the real villain here. But whistleblowers like Tyler Shultz, a Theranos employee who exposed her fraud, caution against buying into the victim narrative. The entire thing is messy, which is resonating with audiences who understand that life operates in the gray, not the black and white. Is it possible to have empathy for Holmes and, at the same time, see her as a manipulator? The movie seems to say yes. Read more on Yahoo! and NPR One of Fielder’s trademarks is his ability to hold a gaze for an excruciatingly long time. Pair that with Holmes and her tendency to do the same, combined with her wide-open eyes and constant nodding, and it’s immensely uncomfortable. Clips and memes of these stare-downs are all over the internet right now. Clinical psychologist and body-language expert Morgan Starr-Riestis has seen the film twice and says it’s unsettling. “When our eyelids are pulled back like that and we’re unblinking, that’s usually a sign of fear or overwhelm,” she told Today. “When you pair it with a smile, the mismatch is naturally unsettling. Our nervous systems just register it as something off.” A psychotherapist on Instagram, Elliot Connie, takes aim at Holmes’s selective nodding and head tilts, which he says are attempts to persuade and control the listener—usually Fielder, and by extension, the audience. Connie says these quirks are employed to make her seem docile and helpless but come off as deliberate and manipulative. Read more on Today and Instagram If you don’t want a spoiler about a major development in the second half of the film, skip to the next section! Everyone else, here we go: Fielder spends much of the movie documenting Holmes in the run-up to her reporting to prison. But things really get intense once she’s inside—and, of course, film crews aren’t allowed in Texas prison camps. So Fielder employs a ringer: Amanda Seyfried, who famously portrayed Holmes in The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu limited series based on the ABC News podcast of the same name. Seyfried doesn’t just read Holmes’s side of her conversations with Fielder—she also becomes part of the story, helping him piece together what’s going on with Evans on the outside. She’s so good at this strange double role that she’s being talked about as a potential Oscar nominee for Best Actress. Read more on The Daily Beast But wait—there’s more! We’ve rounded up additional links to explore if you want to go down the You Can See Everything rabbit hole. articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Put Your Carry-on in Another Passenger’s Overhead Bin?
articles.content:
“Overhead bin space is limited. We’re looking for 10 bags to check at the gate—for free.” I heard the announcement before my recent flight and promptly ignored it. As did everyone else, apparently, because they repeated it at least five more times before boarding. When I got on the plane (in the last boarding group, naturally), the flight attendant grimly told me to stick my carry-on bag wherever I could find a spot. So I spied one about two rows down from the front and played Luggage Tetris until I managed to wedge my bag into a space. Then I took myself and my tiny personal item all the way to the last row of the plane, next to the bathroom, in my seat that didn’t recline.
My daughter was appalled. “Are you even allowed to do that? Don’t people up front pay more for their seats? Isn’t that rude?”
It certainly was allowed—after all, the flight attendant told me to do it. But was it rude? I had to think about that one.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, travel, tech, cleaning, humor and fun facts all week long.
The main reason? Logistics. What happened on my flight isn’t rare. With more and more people choosing to keep their luggage with them, the overhead bin situation is tighter than ever. So when space is limited, you have to take what you can get—even if that means your bag goes in row 2 and you’re seated in row 45. Trying to take your bag farther back when you can see the bins are full (usually indicated by the lids being closed) will cause people to back up behind you and make the boarding process even slower.
Contrary to popular belief, the overhead bins don’t “belong” to a particular seat. “Overhead bin spots are first come, first served, not assigned,” says Loretta Hill, who’s been a flight attendant for more than a decade. It makes more sense to keep your bag close to you, so most people do, but there really aren’t any airline rules that say you have to do so. When bin space is filling up fast, I’d argue it would be rude not to use the first available spot—especially if that’s what the flight attendants are telling you to do.
But this etiquette question isn’t really about what to do when the bins are full. What people are really asking is if it’s OK to put their bag in a front bin when there are plenty of open bins by their seat farther back.
As I sauntered, divinely unencumbered, to my banishment in the last row, I realized why people choose this option even when they don’t have to. Placing your bag in a bin that’s closer to the exit gives you a strategic advantage when it comes time to disembark, helping you get off a little faster. This is especially helpful if you have a tight connecting flight. I also discovered that it means you don’t have to carry your bag as far. And when you’re toting 40 pounds of luggage, every step saved feels like a gift from the normally stingy airline gods.
Just because something is legally allowed, or even encouraged, doesn’t mean everyone considers it polite. (See: Zipper-merging in traffic.) Taking an open spot when things are filling fast and the flight attendant instructs you to is never rude. But taking a bin spot near the front when it isn’t necessary can be rude.
There may also be someone who needs that spot more than you do—perhaps they’re traveling with medical gear, mobility aids, babies or older relatives who need extra help with their luggage. You can’t know who “really” needs the space, so the safest option is just to keep your bag by you. Taking a bin spot that someone else is counting on to have near their seat might also make for some upset feelings or, worst-case scenario, cause a fight. (Which, in this day and age, someone else will then record and post to TikTok, and by the time you land, you’ve become the world’s most hated person online.)
It can also create chaos at the end of the flight. It’s great when your stuff ends up in row 2 while you chill in 45, but if you’re seated in row 2 and you have to put your bag in the bin over row 45, that is decidedly less ideal. You will have to wait politely for everyone else to disembark before you can go back to grab your bag. Or try crowd surfing. (Kidding!) Your “little” bin change can have huge cascading effects if the flight is full, and the truth is that keeping your bag near you makes for a more orderly—ergo, polite—boarding and deplaning process.
There’s also an important exception to the idea that all bins are fair game: Some passengers have actually paid for access to a specific overhead bin or bin area, such as in certain premium cabins. Those areas are usually separated, so you may not even be able to put your bag there. But if you’re tempted to try, don’t. Keep your bag in your own cabin area.
My daughter’s questions were good ones because there’s often a gap between what’s expected and what actually happens. When everyone does what they’re supposed to, public rituals like plane rides, concerts, and urinal selection are seamless. The problem is that this very rarely happens, and sometimes we genuinely don’t know what we’re expected to do. That’s when additional etiquette dilemmas get lobbed at us. Here’s help.
If you’re seated, your bag is already stowed and the person asking is not a flight attendant, you are under no obligation to move it. That said, if they have a good reason and you’re not in a hurry, you could move your bag as a kindness. If it requires a big adjustment and/or they are very insistent, flag down a flight attendant.
Are you a flight attendant? Then, no. Even touching other people’s stuff is iffy, so this is a hard no. If putting your bag in a bin requires any more than a few small adjustments, pick a different spot or ask a flight attendant for help.
It’s not your spot. If you need help finding a good spot for your bag and you don’t see one, politely ask a flight attendant to assist you. Do not remove other people’s bags.
People get mad about the strangest things all the time. It doesn’t mean you have to get mad back. Keeping a cool head when the other person is angry is in my top five peak adulting skills. Usually a little conversation will calm them down, but if it escalates, call a flight attendant and let them handle it.
It’s not rude to put your carry-on in an overhead bin that’s not by your seat, but it’s more polite to keep it near you if that’s an option. Hill agrees: “I’d say it’s rude when you put your bag in the very first bin when you’re seated in the back and there are open bins in the back. Otherwise, it is a shared space, and sometimes it just works out that you’re not near your bag and that’s OK.”
And don’t forget—you do have an easy way out of this situation. Remember the free gate-check offer on my flight that nobody took? Gate-checking may be the politest move on the plane, and it doesn’t even require you to sacrifice your legroom.
Bottom line: The simplest option for everyone is to keep your bag close to you. If that’s not possible, put it in the first spot you see so you don’t impede traffic. And if your bag ends up in first class while you’re wedged into a non-reclining seat next to the bathroom, well, at least one of you had a good flight.

articles.title: 8 Ways Doing a Genealogy DNA Test Can Come Back to Bite You—And Even Cause Legal Problems
articles.content:
We’ve all heard the feel-good stories about DNA testing exonerating the wrongly accused, catching a killer or reuniting long-lost relatives. These situations are often framed by local news anchors and law enforcement as triumphs of technology, and sometimes they are. But voluntarily submitting your DNA to a genealogy testing company—as 21% of Americans have, according to a 2025 YouGov poll—can have unintended consequences.
I can hear you thinking: What could be the harm? I’m not a criminal! And I would love to meet my fourth cousin twice removed! Of course, a family reunion sounds fun (and hopefully you’re not on the FBI’s Most Wanted list), but once you give that spit or swab sample over to one of those companies, the “good” and “bad” tentacles of DNA testing can be impossible to untangle.
“Nobody is against catching serial killers,” says Natalie Ram, a professor of law at the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law whose research focuses on genetic privacy and how it intersects with the criminal legal system. “But privacy is also a really important human value—and an American legal value, in particular.”
I spoke with Ram and Fadi Matthew Kazandji, a criminal defense lawyer and founder and managing partner at Kazandji Law in Canada, to understand the risks of genealogical testing. What could go wrong when you submit your sample to one of these companies? Quite a bit, actually, so read on.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more genealogy, news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
Whether you spit in a cup or swab your cheek, once you send off your sample to a genealogical testing company, “they typically hold onto that biospecimen unless or until you request that they destroy it,” Ram says. And that’s two valuable things the company now has control over: your genetic data and the raw sample, which could be used for further sequencing at a later time.
What kind of further testing are we talking about? One likely candidate is whole-genome sequencing, which gives a much more extensive profile than the typical “genotyping” done by these companies. “The specific details of a specific platform are likely buried in the terms of service and privacy policy, so you should consult that before you use one of their kits,” Ram says.
But, as you’ll see coming up, reading the terms isn’t a fail-safe.
“You should also know that it is extremely common, across the internet, including on these consumer genetics platforms, for a vendor to reserve the right to change the terms of service and privacy policy at any time,” Ram says. “Your continued use of the service, which means your non-deletion of your account, is considered consent to the updated terms.”
And sometimes the companies themselves don’t necessarily think the terms through. She points to the 23andMe bankruptcy from 2025: The company had recently updated their terms to allow the sale of consumer data, but didn’t address the actual physical specimens. That left a kind of “gray zone” about what might happen to them.
“One thing that is quite common in the consumer genetic space is that companies, in their terms of service and privacy policies, often take great pains to say your genetic data is yours,” Ram says. “Which, on the one hand, sounds great. On the other hand, [it] doesn’t actually provide a lot of robust protection.”
She cautions people “not to be wooed” by the language of ownership. Your data and sample may be your “property,” but property rights are not absolute. They’re affected by what you’ve consented to allow others to do with it, which again, is buried in the fine print. “The terms of service will say ‘this is your data,’ but you also grant us all of the rights to do thus and such with it,” Ram says.
This is the one most people are worried about, Ram says, and there have been multiple instances of hacking and other breaches at these companies. A particularly worrisome one affected 23andMe customers of Asian and Ashkenazi Jewish heritage, whose data was sold on the dark web.
The state of California sued 23andMe over this exposure in May 2026. “The sale of this data on the dark web took place amidst a period of mounting anti–Asian American and Pacific Islander and anti-Semitic hate and violence—and explicitly called attention to the deeply personal and identifying nature of that information,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said when announcing the suit.
Remember that unlike a credit card number, you can’t get new DNA. “So once it’s fallen into dark-web hands, it’s there forever and you can’t change it, no matter what,” Ram says.
You’ve probably heard of the Golden State Killer, who eluded capture for decades until 2018, when investigators uploaded a DNA sample to something called GEDmatch. That’s a free database that allows users to upload their genetic data so it can be accessed and searched by others to look for matches.
“Since then, over 1000 cases have been investigated using what is now called forensic investigative genetic genealogy, or FIGG,” Ram says. You might think this is good news (killers off the streets!), but she warns that law enforcement doesn’t always play by the rules and is “largely unburdened by law” in this space.
Let’s say the police are looking for a suspect and they have a DNA sample from a crime scene. “Rather than saying, ‘Hi, I’m law enforcement, and I’d like to search for suspects in your database,’ they will instead pretend to be an ordinary user and say, ‘This is my data,'” Ram says.
After a series of scandals, Ram says GEDmatch created a portal for law enforcement and gave users the option to opt out of allowing investigators to comb through their genetic info. But both law enforcement and genetic genealogists have been caught using loopholes to get around these privacy restrictions.
When 23andMe filed for bankruptcy protection in 2025, the company sold the genetic data of its 15 million–plus users to a new nonprofit created by 23andMe’s co-founder. But the first bidder was a pharmaceutical company called Regeneron, prompting worries from consumers about what they would do with the data and samples.
“It’s unclear whether they were most interested in the user data or the biospecimens, [which] would include not only the information that has already been developed but also all the other information that 23andMe, or whatever platform you’re using, didn’t even sequence yet,” Ram says.
“I am less concerned with insurers trying to get access to these platforms,” Ram says. “I am more concerned about insurers conditioning your ability to get important forms of insurance, like life, long-term-care and disability insurance, based on genetic risks that you knew about because you used one of these services.”
Congress did enact the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA), which protects against discrimination in employment and health insurance under many circumstances. The Affordable Care Act has similar protections. But neither law applies to life, long-term-care and disability insurance, leaving states to create a patchwork of protections.
Kazandji says Canada’s laws are more robust. “It’s a crime here to make someone take a genetic test, or hand over results from one they already took, as a condition of selling them something or signing a contract with them,” he says. “That includes insurance and jobs. The maximum is five years in jail and a $1 million fine, and the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the law in 2020.”
Maybe it sounds exciting to trace your family history, or smart to research potential medical issues in your family tree. But there can be downsides, not the least of which is learning something you wish you hadn’t. “Misattributed paternity is surprisingly common—much more common than people realize,” Ram says. You could learn you have half-siblings, or adoptions that were never disclosed to the family.
Before you use these services, Ram says it’s also important to grapple with the fact that the data you’re sharing is not just your data. “It’s the data of dozens, hundreds or even thousands of other individuals” to whom you’re genetically related. On the other side of the issue, that means even if you haven’t taken one of these tests, your data may still be out there regardless.
It’s easy to say “just don’t take the test,” and that’s one thing to consider. But if you do decide the benefits outweigh the risks, Ram and Kazandji have some advice.
Yes, but slowly, and not always in the direction of stronger privacy.
Ram is very proud of the work she’s done in her state to get protections on the books: “The Maryland law says when law enforcement approaches a person they know to be an innocent third party, to ask them to cooperate in an investigation, they are not allowed to lie.”
Utah is another state that has enacted a “relatively comprehensive regulatory scheme,” Ram says, though it’s less robust than Maryland’s. And Montana has a short statute that requires law enforcement to get a warrant before gaining access to DNA databases.
As for the overall trend with these laws? “I do not have high hopes that they will provide genuine data protection vis-à-vis the government,” Ram says.

She points to the 23andMe bankruptcy from 2025: The company had recently updated their terms to allow the sale of consumer data, but didn’t address the actual physical specimens. That left a kind of “gray zone” about what might happen to them.

“Your data” might not be yours after all

“One thing that is quite common in the consumer genetic space is that companies, in their terms of service and privacy policies, often take great pains to say your genetic data is yours,” Ram says. “Which, on the one hand, sounds great. On the other hand, [it] doesn’t actually provide a lot of robust protection.”

She cautions people “not to be wooed” by the language of ownership. Your data and sample may be your “property,” but property rights are not absolute. They’re affected by what you’ve consented to allow others to do with it, which again, is buried in the fine print. “The terms of service will say ‘this is your data,’ but you also grant us all of the rights to do thus and such with it,” Ram says.

Breaches could expose your sensitive information

This is the one most people are worried about, Ram says, and there have been multiple instances of hacking and other breaches at these companies. A particularly worrisome one affected 23andMe customers of Asian and Ashkenazi Jewish heritage, whose data was sold on the dark web.

The state of California sued 23andMe over this exposure in May 2026. “The sale of this data on the dark web took place amidst a period of mounting anti–Asian American and Pacific Islander and anti-Semitic hate and violence—and explicitly called attention to the deeply personal and identifying nature of that information,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said when announcing the suit.

Remember that unlike a credit card number, you can’t get new DNA. “So once it’s fallen into dark-web hands, it’s there forever and you can’t change it, no matter what,” Ram says.

Law enforcement doesn’t always follow the rules

You’ve probably heard of the Golden State Killer, who eluded capture for decades until 2018, when investigators uploaded a DNA sample to something called GEDmatch. That’s a free database that allows users to upload their genetic data so it can be accessed and searched by others to look for matches.

“Since then, over 1000 cases have been investigated using what is now called forensic investigative genetic genealogy, or FIGG,” Ram says. You might think this is good news (killers off the streets!), but she warns that law enforcement doesn’t always play by the rules and is “largely unburdened by law” in this space.

Let’s say the police are looking for a suspect and they have a DNA sample from a crime scene. “Rather than saying, ‘Hi, I’m law enforcement, and I’d like to search for suspects in your database,’ they will instead pretend to be an ordinary user and say, ‘This is my data,'” Ram says.

After a series of scandals, Ram says GEDmatch created a portal for law enforcement and gave users the option to opt out of allowing investigators to comb through their genetic info. But both law enforcement and genetic genealogists have been caught using loopholes to get around these privacy restrictions.

The company could sell your genetic data

When 23andMe filed for bankruptcy protection in 2025, the company sold the genetic data of its 15 million–plus users to a new nonprofit created by 23andMe’s co-founder. But the first bidder was a pharmaceutical company called Regeneron, prompting worries from consumers about what they would do with the data and samples.

“It’s unclear whether they were most interested in the user data or the biospecimens, [which] would include not only the information that has already been developed but also all the other information that 23andMe, or whatever platform you’re using, didn’t even sequence yet,” Ram says.

Insurance companies could deny coverage

“I am less concerned with insurers trying to get access to these platforms,” Ram says. “I am more concerned about insurers conditioning your ability to get important forms of insurance, like life, long-term-care and disability insurance, based on genetic risks that you knew about because you used one of these services.”

Congress did enact the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA), which protects against discrimination in employment and health insurance under many circumstances. The Affordable Care Act has similar protections. But neither law applies to life, long-term-care and disability insurance, leaving states to create a patchwork of protections.

Kazandji says Canada’s laws are more robust. “It’s a crime here to make someone take a genetic test, or hand over results from one they already took, as a condition of selling them something or signing a contract with them,” he says. “That includes insurance and jobs. You could open up old or unknown family wounds

Maybe it sounds exciting to trace your family history, or smart to research potential medical issues in your family tree. But there can be downsides, not the least of which is learning something you wish you hadn’t. “Misattributed paternity is surprisingly common—much more common than people realize,” Ram says. You could learn you have half-siblings, or adoptions that were never disclosed to the family.

Before you use these services, Ram says it’s also important to grapple with the fact that the data you’re sharing is not just your data. “It’s the data of dozens, hundreds or even thousands of other individuals” to whom you’re genetically related. On the other side of the issue, that means even if you haven’t taken one of these tests, your data may still be out there regardless.

Is there any way to protect yourself from these potential problems?

It’s easy to say “just don’t take the test,” and that’s one thing to consider. But if you do decide the benefits outweigh the risks, Ram and Kazandji have some advice.

  • Make an informed decision. “Think carefully about the choice that you are making, both about whether to use one of these services, and if you do decide to do it, which one you use,” Ram says. Consider the wider exposure your genetic curiosity can bring to others in your family.
  • Read the terms and conditions. “Some of these platforms openly cooperate with law enforcement,” she says. “That might influence your choice.” Others say law enforcement isn’t welcome “but still accept third-party uploads of data (data developed elsewhere), which allows law enforcement to access the data if they lie about who they are.”
  • Be aware of how the privacy settings work. “If your DNA is on GEDmatch, look at your privacy setting, because the names can be confusing,” Kazandji says. “‘Opt-out’ doesn’t take you out of police matching completely.” (Under this setting, your DNA can be used to ID human remains.) “Only ‘Opt-in’ puts you in front of police looking for a suspect in a violent crime, and ‘Private’ takes you out of matching altogether,” he adds.
  • Assert your rights. If law enforcement contacts you, it’s OK to take a step back and consider what to do next. “You can be polite about it,” Kazandji says. “‘I’d like to speak to a lawyer first’ is a full answer.”

Are the laws surrounding genetic testing changing?

Yes, but slowly, and not always in the direction of stronger privacy.

Ram is very proud of the work she’s done in her state to get protections on the books: “The Maryland law says when law enforcement approaches a person they know to be an innocent third party, to ask them to cooperate in an investigation, they are not allowed to lie.”

Utah is another state that has enacted a “relatively comprehensive regulatory scheme,” Ram says, though it’s less robust than Maryland’s. And Montana has a short statute that requires law enforcement to get a warrant before gaining access to DNA databases.

As for the overall trend with these laws? “I do not have high hopes that they will provide genuine data protection vis-à-vis the government,” Ram says.

  • Fadi Matthew Kazandji is a criminal defense lawyer. He is also the founder and managing partner at Toronto’s Kazandji Law, a litigation firm focused on criminal defense, family law and child protection matters.

articles.title: TSA Experts Answer: Can You Wear Your Halloween Costume on a Plane?
articles.content:
Debate time: Would you wear a Halloween costume on a flight? Would you look askance at someone who did? What if they sat right next to you or draped their Morticia Addams wig all over your tray table from the next row up? I have not had the pleasure of sitting next to a costumed Halloween reveler, and due to my rather reserved personality, I can’t imagine wearing one myself, but hey—you be you!
‘Tis the season for fall travel, and during this last stretch of October, there are bound to be people all over this country wondering if the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) will even let them dress up for Halloween on their flights. So, to help all you outgoing types plan around the spooky season, I checked in with someone who knows what he’s talking about: a former TSA official.
“I can tell you that TSA officers have seen just about everything come through a security checkpoint,” says Keith Jeffries, a 20-year veteran of the TSA who is now a vice president at K2 security consultants. “Halloween just makes things a little more interesting.” Ahead, Jeffries and Daniel D. Velez, a current spokesman for the TSA, explain what is and definitely isn’t allowed on planes this Halloween.
Read on to learn what you can wear, what you should pack and what you should leave at home.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more holidays, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
“Absolutely—you can wear a Halloween costume on a flight!” Jeffries says. “TSA doesn’t want to take the fun out of Halloween. The key is making sure your costume doesn’t create a security concern or slow down the screening process.”
As Jeffries mentioned, security is where you’re likely to run into trouble if you show up looking like Vecna from Stranger Things. And being pulled aside for extra screening because you aren’t recognizable as a human being or you’re channeling The Texas Chainsaw Massacre isn’t going to be a good time for anyone (especially the people behind you).
“Halloween is supposed to be scary, but getting through airport security shouldn’t be,” Jeffries says. “My advice is simple: Dress up if you are into the Halloween spirit, but dress to get through security.” Make sure your costume complies with TSA rules (more on that coming up), and be ready to follow any instructions from TSA officers. If you have to take something off, make sure you have room in your bag or time to check it. The last thing you want to do is miss your flight.
“Remember, TSA officers are focused on keeping everyone safe, regardless of whether you’re dressed as a business traveler or Batman,” Jeffries says. “Even superheroes must follow TSA screening procedures. Batman doesn’t get to skip security.”
The main ones are weapons. “Leave the swords, knives, toy guns and realistic-looking weapons and explosive devices at home, or pack permitted costume props in your checked baggage,” Jeffries says. “Even if it’s part of a Halloween costume, anything that looks like a weapon can create a security concern.”
Other items may not be prohibited, but they still have to comply with TSA rules. Here’s what could get you flagged by airport security:
An important reminder: “TSA officers are required to treat potential threats seriously, even on Halloween,” Jeffries says. “If your costume jingles, rattles or lights up like a Christmas tree, don’t be surprised if it gets some extra attention at security.”
It could definitely slow you down. “It’s perfectly fine to dress like a vampire, zombie or your favorite superhero, but TSA still needs to verify your identity,” Jeffries says. “If your costume includes a full-face mask or heavy makeup that makes you difficult to recognize, be prepared to remove the mask or make adjustments so TSA officers can confirm who you are—which can slow down the security process.”
Velez takes it a little further. “Passengers should avoid wearing masks and not have painted faces when going through security screening,” he says. “Officers still need to match travelers to their ID pictures.”
You’d hate to have to take off your Bride of Frankenstein fright wig or wipe off your carefully applied Joker face right when you get to the head of that massive security line. TSA allows colored contacts, but there’s not a lot of guidance on extreme eye-color deviations. So do yourself a favor and wait till you get to your destination to go all-in. And if you’re wearing a mask, stash it in your carry-on or pack it in your luggage.
“TSA needs to know who’s behind the mask,” Jeffries says. (Or the makeup, for that matter.) “Save the big reveal for the Halloween party, not the security checkpoint.”
“The best thing passengers can do is be prepared,” Jeffries says. “Remove bulky costume accessories before screening, keep prohibited items out of carry-on bags and follow the TSA officer’s instructions.” Check the TSA website for the full list of items allowed in carry-on and checked baggage, and build in enough time to deal with any unexpected snags. If there’s any doubt, just leave the questionable item at home.
Velez advises avoiding bulky costumes altogether to get through the Advanced Imaging Technology scanners. Jeffries adds: “My recommendation is to keep your costume simple while going through security and put on the finishing touches after you’ve cleared the checkpoint.”
If you think sharing an armrest is bad, try sharing a row with a guy dressed as Edward Scissorhands. “Think about your entire travel experience, not just getting through TSA,” Jeffries says. “Large costumes, elaborate headpieces and bulky accessories can be uncomfortable on an aircraft and may interfere with other passengers.” (The last thing you want to do is scare a child on a five-hour flight—what if he starts crying?)
“Also, remember that your airline has its own rules regarding attire and what can be brought on board,” Jeffries says. Before you get all decked out, take a peek at your carrier’s website to see if they have specific rules on attire. For example, American Airlines says travelers must “dress appropriately” and not show up in bare feet (sorry, Fred Flintstone). Even if there’s not a specific rule about costumes, remember that airlines have wide latitude to keep disruptions down.
“A little preparation can keep your travel experience from becoming a horror story,” Jeffries says. “Have fun with your costume, use common sense and remember that security is serious business—even when you’re dressed as a clown.”
